claims.text: Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi enhances lattice distortion in FeNiCrMn.
Removing Co modifies the solute–dislocation interaction energy in FeNiCrMn.
The Co-induced changes in lattice distortion and solute–dislocation interactions alter the temperature and strain-rate sensitivity of dislocation mobility.
In Co-free FeNiCrMn, low temperature and high strain rate make dislocation motion more strongly hindered.
Stronger hindrance of dislocation motion at low temperature and high strain rate produces higher strength.
At elevated temperature, thermal activation overcomes dislocation barriers without compromising ductility.
The starting Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is an as-cast, single-phase solid solution.
The controlled comparison is between Co-free FeNiCrMn and equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi processed and tested under identical conditions.
The proposed testing regime spans room temperature to approximately 500 °C and strain rates from approximately 10^-3 s^-1 to above 10^3 s^-1.
Local lattice distortion and solute–dislocation interactions affect dislocation core structure and cross-slip ability.
Changing the local chemical environment changes the energy landscape for dislocation pinning and depinning.
The absence of Co changes dynamic recovery in FeNiCrMn.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have higher yield strength at low temperature and high strain rate.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will show less pronounced softening at elevated temperature.
Co-free FeNiCrMn will preserve a favorable strength–ductility balance at elevated temperature.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi does not exhibit the modified dislocation mobility attributed to Co removal.
The proposed mechanism applies only to as-cast, single-phase solid solutions without significant secondary-phase precipitation.
In situ neutron diffraction, EBSD, and TEM can be used to characterize lattice strain and deformation-related microstructural evolution.
Failure to observe the predicted strength advantage, elevated-temperature strength–ductility advantage, or mechanistic differences would reject the hypothesis.
